data.output: Dew forms when a surface cools the air touching it to its dew point. It is most common on cloudy, calm nights.
data.context: How Dew Forms. Air always contains some water vapour, and the amount it can hold depends on its temperature: the cooler the air, the less vapour it can hold. After sunset, grass, leaves and car roofs lose heat by radiating it up into the sky. On clear nights this cooling is strong, because there are no clouds to send heat back down. As a surface cools, it chills the thin layer of air touching it. When that air reaches its dew point, the temperature at which it can no longer hold all of its water vapour, the extra vapour condenses into droplets on the surface. Still air helps, because wind mixes the cooled layer with the air above. This is why dew is most common on calm, clear nights and is often seen in the early morning. If the dew point is below freezing, the vapour turns straight into ice crystals instead, which we call frost.

data.context: Requests to the Ferrowline API are rate limited per API key. The Starter plan allows 60 requests per minute and the Team plan allows 600. Each response includes the headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset; the last gives the number of seconds until the current window resets. When a key goes over its limit, the API returns status 429 with a Retry-After header. Clients should wait for the number of seconds in Retry-After before trying again, and should back off exponentially if 429 responses keep coming. Bulk endpoints such as /v2/records/batch count as one request but accept at most 500 records per call. Limits apply separately to each key, so several services sharing one key also share one limit.
